lesson.5_1.title: Inflation
lesson.5_1.gut.prompt: A samosa costs ₹15 today. If prices rise 6% every year, what might it cost in 10 years?
lesson.5_1.gut.bridge: Rising prices have a name, and they change how you save.
lesson.5_1.gut.a.label: Still ₹15
lesson.5_1.gut.a.result: Prices rarely stand still for ten years.
lesson.5_1.gut.b.label: About ₹27
lesson.5_1.gut.b.result: Yes. At 6% a year, ₹15 becomes about ₹27 in 10 years.
lesson.5_1.gut.c.label: About ₹60
lesson.5_1.gut.c.result: Not that much. At 6% a year it comes to about ₹27.
lesson.5_1.c1.text: Ask an elder what a cinema ticket cost when they were your age. Then look at the price today.
lesson.5_1.c2.text: Inflation is the rise in prices over time.
lesson.5_1.c3.text: As prices rise, the same money buys less. That is your purchasing power falling.
lesson.5_1.c3.reveal.prompt: With prices rising 7% a year, what will ₹10 lakh buy after 10 years?
lesson.5_1.c4.text: A quick guide is the Rule of 70. Divide 70 by the inflation rate to see how many years prices take to double.
lesson.5_1.c5.text: Your real return is what your money earned, minus inflation.
lesson.5_1.c5.reveal.prompt: Your money earns 6.5% in a year. Prices rise 6%. What is your real return?
lesson.5_1.c5.reveal.answer: 0.5%. You are only a little ahead of prices.
lesson.5_1.c6.text: Money that earns nothing loses buying power every year. Safe from loss is not the same as safe from inflation.
lesson.5_1.q1.right: Yes. Inflation is the general rise in prices.
lesson.5_1.q1.wrong: Inflation is about prices. When prices rise, each rupee buys a little less.
lesson.5_1.q2.prompt: Your savings earn 3% in a year. Prices rise 6%. What is your real return?
lesson.5_1.q2.right: Right: 3% − 6% = −3%. Your money grew, and it still buys less.
lesson.5_1.q2.wrong: Real return is what you earned minus inflation: 3% − 6% = −3%.
lesson.5_1.q3.prompt: ₹1,000 kept in a drawer for 10 years will buy the same things as it does today.
lesson.5_1.q3.right: Correct, it's false. The note is the same. What it buys has shrunk.
lesson.5_1.q3.wrong: It's false. The ₹1,000 stays ₹1,000, but prices rise, so it buys less.
lesson.5_1.effect: Every bucket in your portfolio now carries a real-growth tag: green if it beat inflation, red if it did not.
lesson.5_2.title: Simple and compound interest
lesson.5_2.gut.prompt: You can put aside ₹500 every month. Start now, or wait 2 years?
lesson.5_2.gut.bridge: Time does a lot of the work. Here is how.
lesson.5_2.gut.a.label: Start now
lesson.5_2.gut.a.result: Ten years of saving, at an assumed 8% a year, grows to about ₹92,083. This is an assumption, not a promise.
lesson.5_2.gut.b.label: Wait 2 years
lesson.5_2.gut.b.result: Eight years of saving, at the same assumed 8%, grows to about ₹67,381. The two missing years cost about ₹24,702. This is an assumption, not a promise.
lesson.5_2.c1.text: Interest can earn interest. That one idea changes everything.
lesson.5_2.c2.text: Simple interest is paid only on the money you put in.
lesson.5_2.c2.reveal.prompt: ₹1,000 at 10% a year for 20 years, with simple interest?
lesson.5_2.c2.reveal.answer: ₹3,000 in total: ₹100 a year for 20 years, plus your ₹1,000.
lesson.5_2.c3.text: Compound interest is paid on your money and on the interest it has already earned.
lesson.5_2.c3.reveal.prompt: The same ₹1,000 at 10% a year for 20 years, compounded?
lesson.5_2.c3.reveal.answer: About ₹6,727. More than double the simple-interest total.
lesson.5_2.c4.text: The Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to see how many years money takes to double.
lesson.5_2.c4.reveal.prompt: At 8% a year? At 6% a year?
lesson.5_2.c5.text: Time beats amount. The same monthly sum, started earlier, ends far ahead.
lesson.5_2.c6.text: Compounding works against you too. A debt you do not repay grows the same way.
lesson.5_2.c7.text: Try it: one monthly amount, two starting dates.
lesson.5_2.q1.prompt: What does compound interest earn interest on?
lesson.5_2.q1.right: Yes. Interest joins your money and starts earning too.
lesson.5_2.q1.wrong: Compound interest is paid on your money plus the interest it has already earned.
lesson.5_2.q1.o1: Only the money you put in
lesson.5_2.q1.o2: The money you put in and the interest already earned
lesson.5_2.q2.prompt: At 8% a year, about how long does money take to double?
lesson.5_2.q3.prompt: Starting two years later makes no real difference if you save the same amount each month.
lesson.5_2.q3.right: Correct, it's false. The early years have the longest time to compound.
lesson.5_2.q3.wrong: It's false. The money you save first compounds the longest, so a late start costs more than it seems.
lesson.5_2.effect: When you start a recurring or fixed deposit, a preview shows starting now against starting later.
lesson.5_3.title: Fixed deposits and small savings
lesson.5_3.gut.prompt: You have a ₹6,000 prize. Lock it in a fixed deposit for 6 months, or keep it flexible in savings?
lesson.5_3.gut.bridge: Neither is wrong. They do different jobs.
lesson.5_3.gut.a.label: Fixed deposit
lesson.5_3.gut.a.result: At 6.5% a year it becomes ₹6,195 in 6 months. You cannot touch it early without losing interest.
lesson.5_3.gut.b.label: Keep it in savings
lesson.5_3.gut.b.result: At 3% a year it becomes about ₹6,091 in 6 months. You can take it out any day.
lesson.5_3.c1.text: Some money has to stay within reach. Some can be locked away to earn more.
lesson.5_3.c2.text: A fixed deposit, or FD, takes one lump sum for a fixed tenure at a fixed rate.
lesson.5_3.c3.text: Taking the money out before the tenure ends is a premature withdrawal. The bank then pays a lower rate.
lesson.5_3.c3.reveal.answer: You get ₹6,045: your money back, with interest only at the savings rate.
lesson.5_3.c4.text: The interest you earn is income, and it can be taxed.
lesson.5_3.c5.text: Governments also run small-savings schemes through post offices and banks. Their rates are set by the government every quarter.
lesson.5_3.c6.text: Compare with inflation. Interest of 6.5% while prices rise 6% is a real return of 0.5%.
lesson.5_3.c7.text: An FD suits money you will need on a known date. Your emergency fund has to stay reachable.
lesson.5_3.q1.prompt: What happens if you break a fixed deposit early?
lesson.5_3.q1.right: Yes. Your money is safe. You give up part of the interest.
lesson.5_3.q1.wrong: Your principal comes back. What you lose is interest: the bank pays a lower rate.
lesson.5_3.q1.o2: You get your money back with lower interest
lesson.5_3.q2.prompt: A fixed deposit is a good home for your emergency fund.
lesson.5_3.q2.right: Correct, it's false. An emergency fund must be reachable at once. An FD is locked.
lesson.5_3.q2.wrong: It's false. In an emergency you need the money today, and breaking an FD costs interest.
lesson.5_3.q3.prompt: An FD pays 6.5% a year. Prices rise 6% a year. What is the real return?
lesson.5_3.q3.wrong: Real return is interest minus inflation: 6.5% − 6% = 0.5%.
lesson.5_3.effect: Your Fixed Deposit bucket opens. You choose the amount and the tenure, and breaking it early has a visible cost.
